episodes.title: Niptown half-way lynching
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Niptown half-way lynching was the nonfatal hanging of an accused petty thief by a group that a Nevada newspaper item called "the boys up at Niptown," on a Tuesday in late December 1881, probably December 27. The man was hung up until he was bruised and let live, and the item warned that a further offense would bring his death at the hands of "Judge Lynch." A brief item about it, credited to the Cherry Creek News, circulated in several Nevada papers in the following weeks.

episodes.title: Vigilante hangings near Reynosa, Mexico (1881)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The vigilante hangings near Reynosa were the killings in December 1881 of three men described as 'noted bandits' and of a fourth man, Zefarino Mercado, by Mexican vigilants who called themselves a 'Commission', in Mexico near and south of Reynosa. The news reached American papers through dispatches from Brownsville, Texas, and some later briefs placed the hangings in Brownsville itself.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lincoln County arson suspects (1882)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Lincoln County arson suspects took place in January 1882 in Lincoln County, Georgia, where Black men jailed on an accusation of trying to burn the house of P. A. Cox near Lincolnton were threatened with lynching. County officials kept the prisoners from the threatened lynching, though an Augusta dispatch said fear for their lives persisted.

episodes.title: False report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey
episodes.lead: The false report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey was a January 1882 newspaper story that a mob in Randolph County, West Virginia, had hanged a Black man named Luckey after he shot the white father of the woman he had married. First printed by the Wheeling Register and copied by papers from Virginia to Dakota, the story was called a lie by the Randolph County press within a week. Papers that had carried it then retracted it as 'wholly untrue' or contradicted it.

episodes.title: Rumored lynching of Charles LaFour
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The rumored lynching of Charles LaFour was an unconfirmed report, printed in Wisconsin in early January 1882, that a man known to the Fond du Lac police had killed a man at Superior City on Lake Superior and been lynched by a mob. The story rested on a rumor that the Fond du Lac Commonwealth said it could not verify, and no confirming report appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Hickory church burning
episodes.lead: The Hickory church burning was a night attack at Hickory, Mississippi, in which a Black church was fired into and burned and the town calaboose was burned, around the turn of 1881–82. Three white men and a Black man were arrested on the charges, and a judge went to the town to investigate. The one surviving report, from the Brandon Republican, described a community stirred by lawlessness that its officials had failed to stop.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Coffee in Aubry Valley
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Coffee was a threatened mob killing in Arizona Territory in January 1882, when several men gathered at a saloon to lynch a man named Coffee who had just shot another man. Coffee's friends got him away, and he later surrendered to a deputy sheriff at Murphy's Camp in Aubry Valley. The episode is known from a single brief credited to the Miner, which gives no race for anyone involved.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Daniel Smith
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Daniel Smith was an outbreak of public excitement and talk of lynching in Wayne County, Indiana, in January 1882, after Smith confessed to killing his father, the farmer David H. Smith. Smith, his mother and his brother were held in the county jail at Richmond, and no crowd is reported to have moved against them. Wire services carried the case widely as a "patricide," and a later feature said the son had "narrowly escaped lynching"; no paper stated the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Shooting of Dick Milner
episodes.lead: The shooting of Dick Milner took place in Hickman, Kentucky, probably on Monday, January 30, 1882, when City Marshal Barnes shot Milner, a Black man, in the leg as he ran from arrest. The wound was reported as not dangerous, and the only known account is a brief item in the local Hickman Courier.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Duffy
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Duffy took place on or about January 21, 1882, at Green River (called Blake City in other reports), in Emery County, Utah, after Duffy shot and killed a fellow railroad worker, William Neugent, known as "California Bill." A number of men chased and captured Duffy, and he escaped lynching only through the intercession of others before being held in the Provo jail. None of the reports states the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Neal, Ellis Craft and George Ellis
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Neal, Ellis Craft and George Ellis took place at Catlettsburg, Boyd County, Kentucky, in January 1882, when a large crowd gathered to lynch three white men jailed for the murders of two girls and a boy at nearby Ashland. On January 5 the sheriff took the prisoners down the river by ferry and steamer while the crowd seized the steamer Mountain Girl and gave chase, giving up only when state militia took charge of the prisoners. No one was hurt, the men were lodged in the Maysville jail that night, and within about a month Neal and Craft had been convicted and sentenced to death.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Solomon
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Solomon took place at the Bossier parish jail in Bellevue, Louisiana, in the early hours of January 25, 1882, when ten or twelve unknown men took the jail keys from a deputy sheriff and hanged Solomon, a Black prisoner held on a charge of mule stealing. Hours earlier, by the deputy's account, Solomon had set his cell on fire in an attempt to escape. A coroner's jury found that he died by hanging at the hands of 'parties unknown,' and a Louisiana editor later held up the case as evidence that lynchers spared white criminals.

episodes.title: Wild Horse pay-car incident
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Wild Horse pay-car incident was a confrontation in early January 1882 at Wild Horse station, Texas, in which section hands and laborers on the Texas & Pacific Railway stopped and held the company's pay car. According to a widely reprinted telegraph story, the men took the car for that of General Manager Hoxie, whose order had cut their wages, and threatened to lynch him and burn the car before the paymaster talked them down. No one was hurt, and a Dallas paper gave a different account in which the laborers were demanding unpaid wages and made no lynching threat.

episodes.title: Assault on Ike Johnson
episodes.lead: The assault on Ike Johnson was a roadside attack on a Black man and his wife by two armed white men near the northern edge of Austin, Texas, on the night of January 2, 1882. When Officer J. L. Watts tried to arrest the two men at a house of ill fame later that night, one of them, Emmet McPhail, was shot dead and the other, Jeff Ake, wounded Watts. Papers outside Austin reported the episode as the killing of an ex-convict, and the attack on Johnson was described in detail mainly in the Austin Statesman's inquest coverage.

episodes.title: Seattle lynchings of 1882
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Seattle lynchings of 1882 were the hangings of James Sullivan, William Howard and Benjamin Payne by a citizens' Committee of Safety on Occidental Square in Seattle, Washington Territory, on January 18, 1882. Sullivan and Howard were seized from officers as soon as a justice ended their hearing on a charge of murdering George B. Reynolds, and Payne, held for killing a police officer, was then taken from the county jail. A coroner's jury called the deaths 'speedy and substantial justice', and much of the Pacific Coast press praised the committee.

episodes.title: Killing of Bill Williams (Jim Titus)
episodes.lead: The killing of Bill Williams, also reported as Jim Titus, was the fatal shooting of a Black escaped convict by Memphis police sergeant James Scott at a cabin near Overton station, Tennessee, in mid-January 1882. The officers said he attacked them with an ax when they forced the door, and they left his body where it fell. The Memphis Daily Appeal told the story at length from the officers' side, while papers in Georgia, Texas, Missouri and Mississippi carried a one-sentence wire item.

episodes.title: Killing of Joe Burnes
episodes.lead: The killing of Joe Burnes was the fatal shooting of a Black barber by a police officer in Kansas City, Missouri, reported in a wire dispatch dated January 2, 1882. Officer Lovett, who was said to have mistaken Burnes for a thief, shot him dead when he did not stop, and Lovett was reported exonerated. The item ran as a single paragraph of telegraph news in papers from Texas to Washington.

episodes.title: Posse hanging on Uvas Creek and threatened lynching at Watsonville
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The posse hanging on Uvas Creek and threatened lynching at Watsonville took place in January 1882, when a California deputy sheriff's posse hunting the men wanted for the stabbing of Charles Rossi strung up an unnamed man, called a Mexican in one dispatch, to make him reveal where the fugitives were hiding. The posse then captured Ignacio Tejada at a hollow tree, and friends of Rossi at Watsonville threatened to lynch the prisoners before officers sent them to Santa Cruz by train. The hanged man survived and the prisoners were not lynched; Tejada was later sentenced to seven years in San Quentin.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Wagoner
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Wagoner took place at Ironton, Lawrence County, Ohio, shortly after midnight on the night of January 19, 1882, when forty to sixty masked men took him from the county jail and hanged him from a tree in the court-house yard. Wagoner was charged with murdering Dr. Joseph A. Beggs; his co-accused, William Zeek, was strung up by the same band and returned to jail after a forced confession. No one was arrested, and Ohio papers divided over whether the hanging was justified.

episodes.title: Killing of Marshal Smith
episodes.lead: The killing of Marshal Smith was the fatal shooting of a Black preacher at his door on Carruthers' plantation at Clinton, Louisiana, on a Thursday night in late January 1882. Two white men, named in the dispatches as McKee and Singlebarre or Singlebury, were arrested for the murder on circumstantial evidence. The case reached the national press only as a brief wire item, and no later report of its outcome was found.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of McBride at Waterloo, Illinois
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of McBride took place at Waterloo, Monroe County, Illinois, in late January 1882, when a crowd gathered near the jail holding a young pupil accused of stabbing his schoolteacher to death. The crowd threatened to lynch him but made no attempt to do so, and no one was harmed. The killing of the teacher was carried widely as a crime item, while the threat at the jail appeared in a single regional paper, and no report gives the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jake Lewis and others at Graball, Texas
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Jake Lewis and others at Graball, Texas, was a reported threat by local citizens in January 1882 against Black men arrested for the murder and beheading of Jordan Thompson, a Black man. No lynching took place; Lewis pleaded guilty, was held in jail, and in April was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to twenty years. The threat is known only from a telegraphic brief, while the local paper described an excited crowd held back from the courthouse by guards.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Seymour in Rock Falls, Illinois
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Seymour took place in the village of Rock Falls, Whiteside County, Illinois, on the night of Monday, January 30, 1882, when twenty to thirty men went to the house of a man named Seymour intending to lynch him. Seymour and his wife were accused of beating, starving and otherwise abusing a seven-year-old girl who lived in their household, and both had fled before the men arrived. A dispatch from nearby Sterling carried the story to papers from Pennsylvania to California, most of which dwelt on the cruelty charged against the couple rather than on the lynching party.

episodes.title: Mob attack on Sheriff J. H. Hutchinson at Washington, Texas
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The mob attack on Sheriff J. H. Hutchinson took place at Washington, Washington County, Texas, on January 24, 1882, when a crowd turned on the county sheriff after a constable held for murder escaped from his custody. The crowd cursed and assaulted him, and by one account brought a rope and nearly hanged him before cooler heads intervened. Hutchinson survived and was later indicted for negligently permitting the escape.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Smith in San Antonio
episodes.lead: The police shooting of Smith in San Antonio took place on the morning of January 7, 1882, when Policeman Martinez shot a Black man named Smith in the hip while arresting him as a suspected robber. Smith survived with a flesh wound and was jailed. The case drew a local editorial in the San Antonio Evening Light that criticized arming the police and said Martinez faced a charge of assault with intent to murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Sylvester Henderson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Sylvester Henderson took place in St. Louis, Missouri, on the evening of January 24, 1882, when a crowd put a rope around the neck of Henderson, an ash gatherer said to have fatally cut a man named Richard Hinch. Policemen took Henderson to the station before the crowd could hang him, and he survived. The episode reached print as a single brief wire item, which gave no one's race.

episodes.title: Lynching of W. E. Graham
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of W. E. Graham took place on the night of January 2, 1882, when masked men took Graham from the jail at Ellsworth, Kansas, and hanged him from a telegraph pole. Graham was accused of killing and robbing his uncle, Philip Egley, at Venango in Ellsworth County and burning his house, and he was reported to have confessed in jail. The men went back for a second prisoner, W. C. Rose, but officers had already moved him. A brief wire dispatch carried the hanging to newspapers across the country, and the inquest verdict drew sarcastic comment as far away as Virginia.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Steele
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Steele took place on the night of January 28, 1882, about twelve miles from Logansport, Indiana, when neighbors of a farm woman, Mrs. Buell, pursued and hanged Steele, a man described as a tramp. He was accused of assaulting her after asking for supper, and after the hanging his pursuers piled brush around his body and burned it. A Cincinnati wire dispatch carried the story across the country, often under headlines that called the killing deserved.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of "Majah" Alford
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of "Majah" Alford took place on Sunday, February 12, 1882, when a crowd of about fifty went to the jail at Gainesville, Texas, intending to seize Alford, a Black music teacher accused of attempting to rape a fourteen-year-old girl. The crowd confined itself to talk and threats and withdrew when the jail guards refused it, and Alford remained in custody to await trial. The episode is known from a single item in the Waco Daily Examiner, which quoted the Gainesville Hesperian.

episodes.title: Watertown posse pursuit of a Black barber (1882)
episodes.lead: The Watertown posse pursuit of a Black barber was a manhunt in Watertown, apparently in Dakota Territory, reported in February 1882, in which a citizens' posse pursued an unnamed Black barber accused of attempting to rape a local woman. The single report said that he would be dealt with summarily if caught, but it gave no outcome, and no later report was found.

episodes.title: Mock hanging of five men at Las Vegas, New Mexico
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The mock hanging of five men at Las Vegas, New Mexico, took place about midnight on Saturday, 4 February 1882, when a group of East Side citizens seized Cal. Jones, Tobe Johnson, Ed. Patters and two men known as Roxy and Buck and pulled each of them up by a noose. The men were released alive and left town, and the Las Vegas Daily Gazette praised the act as a lesson to "thugs and dead-beats."

episodes.title: Lynching of Deering
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Deering was the hanging of a young prisoner named Deering by a mob in western Coryell County, Texas, in February 1882, after he was taken from the officer carrying him to the Gatesville jail. Days later armed men from his home neighborhood rode into Gatesville and demanded the arrest of the lynchers, and the sheriff jailed a man named Leverett and his two sons. That reversal, with the victim's neighbors threatening to take the law into their own hands against a lynch mob, carried the story by wire to papers across the country.

episodes.title: Lawrenceville grave-dancing deaths
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Lawrenceville grave-dancing deaths were the deaths of three young men at Lawrenceville, Illinois, reported in February 1882, who fled from mourners preparing to lynch them after they had danced at a friend's grave. Escaping down the river in a leaky boat, they were left stranded on the bank when it sank, and they were found dead of cold and exhaustion. The story circulated as a short unsigned paragraph in miscellany columns from February to May 1882.

episodes.title: Centreville roadside ambush
episodes.lead: The Centreville roadside ambush was a shooting near Centreville, Texas, in February 1882, in which a white man named Lyle fired from hiding on two Black men named Hall and their wives as they rode in a wagon. Both men were killed and both women were reported mortally wounded. Carried by a St. Louis telegraph dispatch, the story ran in papers from West Virginia to California under headlines such as "Negroes Waylaid and Shot" and "Double Murder."

episodes.title: Lynching of J. O. Weldon
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of J. O. Weldon took place at Hackberry, Arizona Territory, about thirty miles from Mineral Park, on the night of February 21, 1882, when a party of fifteen men took Weldon from custody and hanged him from the beam of a blacksmith shop. Weldon had been accused of shooting and killing John Bullock, a stage driver, in a Hackberry saloon the day before. The story ran across the country as the lynching of a "desperado", and no article states the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Beating of Jim Dunlap aboard the steamer James Lee
episodes.lead: The beating of Jim Dunlap aboard the steamer James Lee took place near Memphis, Tennessee, on the night of February 7, 1882, when the boat's crew attacked Dunlap, a Black deck passenger they accused of pushing the second mate overboard. He was beaten so badly that his life was despaired of before the boat's officers could reach him. The episode survives only as a short wire paragraph reprinted in small-town papers across several states.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Redden
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of James Redden was a reported effort by residents of the Odessa and Middletown area of New Castle County, Delaware, to lynch Redden, a Black man accused of raping a young girl, on 24–25 February 1882. Wilmington dispatches said officers resisted an organized attempt and took him safely to New Castle jail, but the local Middletown Transcript denied that any attempt was made. Redden was later tried, convicted of rape and hanged at New Castle on 25 August 1882.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Adams
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Adams was the hanging of a man described as 'a half-breed Mexican' by about thirty of his neighbors near Pit River in Big Valley, Lassen County, California, on the night of February 24, 1882. Accused of horse stealing, Adams had defied a committee that ordered him to leave, and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union reported the killing as the work of 'the Vigilantes'.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Philander Husted
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Philander Husted took place in February 1882 at the jail where Husted, a young man of South Toledo, Ohio, was held on an accusation of raping a young girl named Long. A crowd gathered to lynch him and a rope was secured, but no attack followed, and Husted survived an attempt to take his own life. Neither report found states his race.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Lyle
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Thomas Lyle took place in Smyth County, Virginia, in February 1882, after James N. Mercer was shot dead near Town House in a quarrel with Lyle and his brother over Mercer's canoe. According to a Lynchburg dispatch, the sheriff rescued Lyle just as a mob was about to hang him from a tree, while the Bristol News said local citizens were restrained with difficulty from lynching both brothers after they were jailed at Marion. Lyle was convicted of second-degree murder in late April and sentenced to eighteen years in the penitentiary. None of the reports stated the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Threats against Mormon missionaries in Union County, Tennessee
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threats against Mormon missionaries in Union County, Tennessee, were threats of lynching reported in February 1882 against Mormon missionaries who had won converts, some of them Black, in Union County in East Tennessee. No violence was reported, and the episode is known only from a short Chattanooga dispatch and Tennessee rewrites of it.

episodes.title: Masked raid on Berry Lawrence's house
episodes.lead: The masked raid on Berry Lawrence's house was a night attack by four masked men on the home of a Black man near Cuthbert, Randolph County, Georgia, on Tuesday, 28 February 1882. Lawrence shot the first raider through the broken door, and the dead man was unmasked as Leonidas Bailey, a young white man of the county. A coroner's jury called the killing justifiable homicide, and the wire story of a Black householder killing a masked white raider ran in papers from Washington to Texas.

episodes.title: Whipping of Pat Bowen
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The whipping of Pat Bowen was an assault in early 1882 near Devils River in Kinney County, Texas, in which unnamed captors thrashed Bowen, a man described as a tramp, shaved off half his hair and moustache, and threatened to lynch him. The attack followed a man named Bell's accusation that Bowen had robbed and beaten him, and Bowen was later arrested and released in San Antonio.

episodes.title: Nashville police shooting of a fleeing Black man (1882)
episodes.lead: The Nashville police shooting of a fleeing Black man took place in Nashville, Tennessee, on a Tuesday in mid-February 1882, apparently February 14, when a policeman fired at a man running from him. The bullet missed, and no one was hurt. The Memphis Daily Appeal noted the incident chiefly to remark that an officer who killed a fleeing person who was not a felon could be prosecuted for murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of R. D. Raven
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of R. D. Raven took place at Waverly, Lancaster County, Nebraska, on the night of February 20, 1882, when a crowd seized Raven, who was accused of shooting James Cook dead in a dispute over the spelling of a word, and put a rope over his head. Sheriff Ensign and Deputy Sheriff Mellick got him away from the crowd and took him to the jail at Lincoln on a passing special train. Papers across the country treated it as a curiosity, a killing over spelling that nearly ended in a hanging; none gave the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Spain at Newberry, South Carolina
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Spain at Newberry, South Carolina, took place in February 1882, when a white traveling seed seller accused of insulting a planter's wife was pursued, jailed and threatened by local men. A sheriff's guard foiled a plan to take him from jail and whip him, and a trial justice ordered him released.

episodes.title: Lynching of Theodore Burton
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Theodore Burton was the hanging of a jailed man by fifty masked men near Belgreene, Alabama, reported in a Montgomery dispatch dated February 23, 1882. Burton, accused of killing John Rockard with an axe, was taken from jail after the men forced the sheriff to give up the keys, and his body was found hanging from a tree the next morning. Northern dailies printed the dispatch as the lynching of a "desperado" or "murderer," and weekly crime digests carried a brief version into March.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Medley
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Medley took place in the Bear Quarter section of Norfolk County, Virginia, on about February 10, 1882, when residents tried to lynch a Black man accused of assaulting a five-year-old girl. Constable David Sykes got him to jail, and a Norfolk dispatch noted that the angry residents included both whites and Black people. Medley was later tried in the county court and sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Killing of William Rice
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of William Rice was the reported death of Wm. Rice, described as an alleged revenue informer, whose body was rumored in early February 1882 to have been found in Gwinnett County, Georgia, cut nearly in two. The only report, a one-sentence item in the Savannah Morning News, presented the story as a rumor and named no killers, motive or race.

episodes.title: Lynching of Wm. Smeal
episodes.lead: The lynching of Wm. Smeal was the hanging of a Black farm worker by a mob near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road in Gwinnett County, Georgia, in mid-February 1882. Accused of stealing a horse, Smeal was taken from his cabin at night, whipped until he confessed, and hanged from a black-jack tree, where his body was found the next day. A short Athens dispatch carried the story nationally, and the local Jefferson Herald, while calling horse stealing a grave offense, condemned the killing as lynch law.

episodes.title: Sycamore station lynching threat
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Sycamore station lynching threat was a gathering of about 300 people at Sycamore station, in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, on February 6, 1882, who meant to lynch W. H. Yeatts, a prisoner accused of murdering a local merchant there four days earlier. Warned of the crowd, officers at Lynchburg held Yeatts back and that evening sent him to the county jail at Chatham on a train that did not stop at Sycamore. The Associated Press carried the story nationally as a murderer's narrow escape, and Yeatts was later tried, convicted and hanged at Chatham in August 1882.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Edward Alberson and James Eato
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Edward Alberson and James Eato took place at the railroad depot in Roslyn, Long Island, New York, on the night of March 25, 1882, when a crowd threatened to lynch the two Black prisoners as officers removed them to the Queens County Jail. The officers got the men onto the train, and both later stood trial in Long Island City. The threat appears in a single New-York Tribune report on a robbery case that the paper followed closely.

episodes.title: Del Norte jail attack (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Del Norte jail attack was a night assault on the jail at Del Norte, Colorado, on Saturday, March 4, 1882, by about a hundred men said to be stockmen, who shot two prisoners charged with cattle stealing, Arnold Howard and Frank Young. A Denver dispatch carried nationally reported Howard killed and Young mortally wounded, and many papers headlined it as a lynching of cattle thieves. A news item two months later said instead that Howard had escaped the mob and been captured near Pueblo, leaving the outcome in doubt.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Sarver
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bob Sarver was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob near Franklin, Simpson County, Kentucky, on the night of Monday, March 6, 1882. Accused of attempting to rape a 16-year-old white girl, Sarver was taken from officers who were moving him by train and was hanged from a tree at the scene of the alleged attempt. A one-line Nashville dispatch carried the case to papers across the country, and three men were later reported arrested for the killing.

episodes.title: Lynching of C. D. Owens
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of C. D. Owens took place in Tampa, Florida, on March 6, 1882, when a mob took Owens, a young white man from London, from the jail and hanged him from a shade tree in front of the court house. Owens had been jailed about an hour earlier, accused of breaking into a house and attacking a young woman with a knife. Papers stressed that it happened in daylight beside the federal court, and Judge Locke later disbarred a Tampa attorney, Gen. Joseph B. Wall, for aiding it.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Daniel Wagner
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Daniel Wagner took place on Sunday, March 12, 1882, in Park Place, Scranton, Pennsylvania, when a crowd surrounded a barn where Wagner, a fifty-five-year-old man accused of assaulting an eight-year-old girl, was hiding. Wagner was arrested and jailed, and no one was reported hurt. The papers carried the episode only as a brief wire dispatch, and none of them identified Wagner's race.

episodes.title: Killing of Elbert Rogers
episodes.lead: The killing of Elbert Rogers was the fatal shooting of a Black man accused of horse theft in Henderson County, Texas, in March 1882. Rogers was shot in the back while being pursued by a deputy sheriff and the horse's owner and died in the jail at Athens, and a coroner's jury attributed the shot to an unknown hand.

episodes.title: Killing of Thomas Edmondson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of Thomas Edmondson was the fatal shooting of a citizen of Good Hope, a village near Macomb, Illinois, on the night of Friday, March 17, 1882, by three men he had earlier turned over to the police. The accused gunman, Ed. Gick, was arrested, and a Chicago dispatch reported that people were restrained only with difficulty from lynching him. Gick was convicted of murder that September, and the judge's handling of his sentence caused an outcry in McDonough County.

episodes.title: Beating of William Emery
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The beating of William Emery was an assault on a jailed man in Holden, Missouri, on the night of about March 9, 1882, when a party of ten citizens took him from the town calaboose and horsewhipped him. The town marshal, H. H. Still, was suspected of leading the party and left town after Emery's neighbors threatened to mob him. Several men were later arrested, and all were acquitted at a hearing before a Holden justice.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Emma Johnson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Emma Johnson took place at Summerfield, Georgia, about six miles from Macon, in March 1882, when a mob surrounded the officers holding Johnson, a young Black woman accused of killing a local merchant. The officers prevented the lynching and took her to Macon, where she was later convicted of murder in Bibb Superior Court. Papers across the country carried the story as a murder, with the mob mentioned in a single sentence.

episodes.title: Killing of escaped convicts near Big Springs, Texas (1882)
episodes.lead: The killing of escaped convicts near Big Springs, Texas, took place in March 1882, when rangers pursuing four Black convicts who had escaped from a Texas & Pacific Railroad work gang killed two of them and captured the other two. The convicts were said to have killed a guard in the escape, and the episode ran as a brief wire item in papers from Texas to West Virginia, Utah and California.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of F. H. Moberay
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of F. H. Moberay took place at Caracas, Colorado, in March 1882, when a crowd of Mexicans threatened to lynch a Denver & Rio Grande Railroad employee who had shot two Mexican men, killing one, in a dispute over a debt. Moberay was taken to the Chama jail for safety and escaped from it. The story reached the press as a single Denver wire dispatch, reprinted across the country for a few days.

episodes.title: Burning of Floyd King's house
episodes.lead: The burning of Floyd King's house was a suspected arson in early March 1882 in which the house of Floyd King, a Black man, was burned in Oconee, apparently Oconee County, Georgia. Two white tramps were thought to be responsible, but no arrest was reported, and the burning is known only from one short paragraph in the Savannah Morning News.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at Cedar Rapids, Iowa (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching at Cedar Rapids, Iowa, took place on March 2, 1882, when an excited mob set out to lynch a gambler accused of shooting saloon keeper Josh Fuller. The accused was hurried to jail before the mob could act, and the episode survives only as a brief wire item that names no one's race.

episodes.title: Burning of Isham Edwards's fence and mule
episodes.lead: The burning of Isham Edwards's fence and mule was a pair of night-time attacks in March 1882 on the farm of Isham Edwards, a Black tenant on the Papy place, six miles from Tallahassee, Florida. Unidentified attackers burned about fifty panels of his fence on 11 March and the next night set his mule on fire in its stable, injuring the animal badly. The Weekly Floridian of Tallahassee condemned the attack on the mule as "fiendish cruelty," and the item was reprinted in Savannah.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas C. Early
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Thomas C. Early took place in Leadville, Colorado, on March 28, 1882, after Early, a local lawyer and politician, shot and killed police officer Samuel Townsend. Wire reports said an attempt to lynch Early was frustrated, and a Missouri paper reported that he was kept under strong guard at the jail against a mob that threatened to lynch him. An inquest jury recommended that Early be held for the grand jury without bail.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Lacy and Robert Rodrick
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of James Lacy and Robert Rodrick was the hanging of two prisoners by masked men at Rawlins, Wyoming Territory, in the early morning of March 19, 1882. A third prisoner, William Carter, escaped and later shot at a deputy who tried to recapture him. The story ran nationally in two wire versions that disagreed on the date and on the crimes the men were accused of.

episodes.title: Killing of James M. Davis
episodes.lead: The killing of James M. Davis was the ambush shooting of a deputy United States revenue collector by a concealed party of men described as moonshiners, on the Beersheba road about three miles from McMinnville, Warren County, Tennessee, on the afternoon of March 13, 1882. Davis, known as a 'celebrated raider of moonshiners,' was shot from his horse and finished with shots to the head, and the papers reported between twenty and more than thirty bullet wounds. The federal revenue service offered rewards for the killers, but no arrest appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Assault on John H. Dorsey
episodes.lead: The assault on John H. Dorsey was an attack by a crowd on a Black man in Washington, D.C., on the afternoon of 17 March 1882. Three men named as members of the crowd were brought before the Police Court the next morning, where one was discharged and two were sentenced. The case drew only brief notices in two Washington evening papers.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Redmond, Charles Shelton and Harry French
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Redmond, Charles Shelton and Harry French took place at Los Lunas, New Mexico, in early March 1882, when masked men took the three prisoners from the jail and hanged them from the nearest trees. The same mob took two Black prisoners from the jail, beat them and turned them loose. The story spread nationwide through an Albuquerque special to the Denver Republican, which presented the three hanged men as murderers.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of H. C. Laws
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of H. C. Laws was an attack on the night of Saturday, March 11, 1882, in which masked, armed men entered Greenman's Hotel in Linkville, Lake County, Oregon, to seize Laws, a prisoner charged with the murder of a boy named Frank Calavan. They left without the prisoner, but in an exchange of gunfire they killed Deputy Sheriff J. F. Lewis and wounded Justice Wright. The death of an officer defending a prisoner from lynchers was carried by wire across the country, and western papers followed the search for the mob into April.

episodes.title: Arkadelphia road-work shooting
episodes.lead: The Arkadelphia road-work shooting was a shooting affray in early March 1882, six miles south of Arkadelphia, Arkansas, in which two white men, Joe Ross and Bud Henry, shot three Black men, Lewis Smith, Aaron Clark and Ed Clark. Smith was killed outright and a second man was reported unable to recover, though one later roundup said all three died. The two white men escaped, and the story ran as a brief wire item from Memphis to Minnesota and Wisconsin.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lucian Langdon and William Harrison
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lucian Langdon and William Harrison took place at Prineville, Wasco county, Oregon, early on Friday, March 17, 1882, when masked men overpowered a deputy sheriff's guard, shot Langdon and hanged Harrison from a bridge. Langdon had been arrested on the charge of killing two neighbors in a land dispute, while papers reported that nothing connected Harrison, his employee, to the killings. The wire account ran nationally, sometimes under headlines calling Harrison innocent.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Moon brothers
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of the Moon brothers was a failed effort by a mob to seize and lynch two or more prisoners held in the jail at Gadsden, Alabama, in March 1882. The mob could not cross the river to reach the jail, and the authorities then moved the prisoners to Birmingham under military guard.

episodes.title: Killing of Munroe Bloom
episodes.lead: The killing of Munroe Bloom was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a Georgia constable at Morrow's Station, on the Central railroad, in mid-March 1882. The constable had warrants charging Bloom and a second Black man with forgery, and Bloom, shot as he resisted arrest, was later found dead in the woods. A coroner's jury ruled the killing justifiable homicide, and the Atlanta dispatch reporting it ran in papers from Richmond and New York to Texas.

episodes.title: Third Creek riot
episodes.lead: The Third Creek riot was a fight between whites and Black men at Third Creek station on the Western North Carolina Railroad on Saturday, March 11, 1882. About a hundred people took part, some with pistols and shotguns, and several Black men were badly but not fatally shot. A Salisbury militia company ended the fighting and jailed twenty-four rioters, and a Raleigh dispatch carried the story to papers across the country under headlines such as "Negroes Rioting in North Carolina."

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Taylor in the Maryland Penitentiary
episodes.lead: The killing of Robert Taylor took place on the afternoon of March 1, 1882, when James Byrne, an officer of the Maryland penitentiary in Baltimore, shot dead Taylor, a Black convict, in the prison foundry. A coroner's jury ruled the same day that Byrne had acted in self-defense, and the story ran in short wire items as the shooting of an insubordinate convict.

episodes.title: Sunflower Landing smallpox shooting
episodes.lead: The Sunflower Landing smallpox shooting was an attack on an unnamed Black man ill with smallpox, who was shot and whose cabin was burned at Sunflower Landing, Mississippi, as reported in March 1882. The only known account was a single line in a Kentucky paper's news column, which did not say who carried out the attack, when it happened, or whether the man survived.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jack and Manuel Brown
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jack and Manuel Brown was an unsuccessful attempt, on the night of March 1, 1882, at Lexington, Mississippi, to lynch two young Black men charged with attacking the storekeeper A. H. Pinkston. The attempt failed, and the only report of it was a single sentence in a Mississippi weekly's column of state news.

episodes.title: Abduction of Walter Saunders
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The abduction of Walter Saunders was the seizure of a young man from Atchison, Kansas, by a party of men in a Kansas City saloon in March 1882; he was not seen again. His captors accused him of assaulting a thirteen-year-old girl and hurried him toward the Kaw bridge, and it was supposed he had been thrown into the river.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Stock
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Stock took place in Kansas City, Missouri, on March 29, 1882, when about one thousand friends of a man shot dead in Stock's West Kansas City saloon tried to lynch Stock after his capture. Officers got the prisoner into jail, where he was reported safely confined. The story ran as a short wire item, and one printing gave the prisoner's name as "William Mack".

episodes.title: Lynching of William Parish
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Parish was the killing of a prisoner by masked men in Newellton, Tensas Parish, Louisiana, on a Friday night in late February or March 1882. Parish, accused of shooting Sol. Waters over a deer skin, was taken from his chain and hanged in town. A coroner's jury found he died by strangulation at the hands of men unknown.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph from Raleigh County, West Virginia
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph was the beating and driving out of a Black schoolteacher by a mob in Raleigh County, West Virginia, reported in February 1882. According to Randolph's own statement, the mob beat him and ordered him to leave after a justice acquitted men he had had arrested, and he left to save his life. A Parkersburg paper headed its notice of the case "SHAMEFUL" while qualifying its comment on whether the statement was true.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Patrick Simpson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Patrick Simpson was a pair of mob threats in 1881 against a man from Fulton, New York, who had been brought to Richmond, Kentucky, under arrest after he was mistaken for a fugitive murderer named Rogers. A mob tried to lynch him when he arrived, and after a court discharged him a crowd surrounded the court-house; he escaped on foot and reached home about the start of 1882. Papers told it as a story of mistaken identity and a narrow escape, and none of them gave Simpson's race.

episodes.title: Lynching of Peter Corbin
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Peter Corbin was the reported killing of a prisoner taken from the Gilmer county jail at Ellijay, Georgia, by a party of masked men in early 1882. Corbin, charged with an outrage on a lady, was reported found the next day in woods near the town with his head severed from his body. The only account is a short item from the Dalton Citizen, which passed the story on as something it had learned and hoped was untrue.
